name: keras
title: Keras: A Multi-Backend Deep Learning Framework for AI
answer: Keras is an open-source Python deep learning framework maintained by the Keras team, released under the Apache 2.0 licence and described as deep learning for humans. It sits at the model-building layer of the AI stack, offering high-level APIs for defining, training and serving neural networks. Since version 3.0 it runs on JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch or OpenVINO, so the one thing to know before adopting it is that the same code can target several backends, though performance varies by model and hardware.

sections.body: Keras is a Python deep learning framework made by the Keras team and hosted at github.com/keras-team/keras, with its official site at keras.io. It is licensed under Apache 2.0 and its repository has accumulated roughly 64,000 stars, with the last recorded push in October 2026. It occupies the model-building layer of the AI stack, the level at which a developer defines layers, losses, optimizers and training loops rather than the numerical kernels underneath. The 3.0 release, announced on the official site, reframed it as a multi-backend framework: Keras workflows can run on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO for inference only. The site states that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Keras covers the concrete jobs of deep learning work: training, evaluation and inference through fit(), evaluate() and predict(), data handling through NumPy arrays, tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects and Pandas dataframes, and model definition through the Sequential, functional and subclassing APIs. The functional API handles non-linear topology, shared layers and multiple inputs or outputs, which makes it suitable for autoencoders and multi-branch models, while the Sequential API suits a plain stack of layers with one input and one output tensor. The site's examples extend to generative work, including a mini-GPT text generation tutorial built with KerasHub, and to transfer learning recipes for image data. Keras is strongest where a readable, high-level model definition matters and where the same code should be portable across backends. The official benchmarks note that JAX typically delivers the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU and CPU, though results vary from model to model and non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed for approachability, and the official guides walk a beginner from loading the MNIST dataset through reshaping arrays, compiling a model with a loss, optimizer and metrics, and calling fit(). The functional API guide explains that batch size is omitted when specifying input shapes, only the shape of each sample is given, and that a Model is created by naming its inputs and outputs. The Sequential guide notes that layers generally need to know their input shape before weights are created, and recommends specifying that shape in advance. What the site does not spell out is the mathematical background a reader needs for deeper work, such as understanding loss functions, gradient behaviour or distribution strategies. The guides assume comfort with Python and with array-shaped thinking, and the custom loss examples use operations such as ops.mean and ops.square, so some familiarity with tensor operations helps. The official material offers runnable examples and API references rather than a structured course, so a student should expect to learn by running code.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around Keras is broad and documented on the official site. Keras 3 implements the full Keras API across TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch, including over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, training and evaluation loops, and saving and serialization infrastructure. The keras.ops namespace provides cross-backend operations such as ops.matmul, ops.sum, ops.stack and ops.einsum, plus neural network functions such as ops.softmax, ops.binary_crossentropy and ops.conv, and custom layers written only with these operations work across JAX, PyTorch and TensorFlow from the same code. KerasHub supplies pretrained components, including the TokenAndPositionEmbedding and TransformerDecoder layers used in the mini-GPT example. The keras.distribution namespace handles model and data parallelism, currently implemented for the JAX backend with TensorFlow and PyTorch described as coming soon. The repository's star count and the site's claim of over 2.5 million developers indicate a large user base, and the guides, examples and API references form the core of the official support.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both quick experiments and production use, and the trade-offs are visible in the official material. On the prototyping side, a model can be created by passing a list of layers to the Sequential constructor or incrementally with add() and pop(), and default optimizer, loss and metrics can be specified through string identifiers as a shortcut. The functional API supports saving an entire model as a single file, including the optimizer and its state, so training can resume where it left off. On the production side, Keras 3 offers backend choice, and the site reports that JAX typically gives the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU and CPU, with results varying by model. The distribution API supports model parallelism, data parallelism and combinations of both, though it is currently implemented only for JAX. The cost of this flexibility is that performance is not uniform: the same model can behave differently across backends, and the site itself notes that non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU. A reader should treat backend selection as a tuning decision rather than a fixed property.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The official site states that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine, which places it among the widely used frameworks rather than a niche or legacy choice. The repository's roughly 64,000 stars and its active push history in October 2026 support the picture of a maintained project. For someone choosing what to learn for work, that adoption matters because Keras skills transfer across the TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch ecosystems through the shared API and the keras.ops namespace. The site also notes that existing tf.keras models using only built-in layers can start running in JAX and PyTorch right away, which lowers the cost of moving an existing codebase. What the facts and the site do not provide is a breakdown of job roles, salary data or employer demand, so any career judgement beyond the named adopters and developer count would be speculation.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is a Python framework, and its polyglot pattern is unusual because it sits above other frameworks rather than replacing them. A Keras model can be instantiated as a PyTorch Module, exported as a TensorFlow SavedModel, or instantiated as a stateless JAX function, and the site describes Keras as usable as a low-level cross-framework language for developing custom components such as layers, models or metrics that then run in native JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch workflows from one codebase. Training routines accept tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects, NumPy arrays and Pandas dataframes regardless of backend. In practice this means a team can keep its existing TensorFlow or PyTorch serving and data pipelines while writing model code once in Keras. The site does not describe integrations with languages outside Python, so the framework should be understood as a Python layer within a multi-backend stack rather than a language-neutral runtime.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The official material is candid about several limits. The distribution API is currently implemented for the JAX backend only, with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon, so model and data parallelism are not yet uniform across backends. Backend performance varies from model to model, and the site notes that non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU, which means benchmark results cannot be generalised. The Sequential API is explicitly not appropriate for non-linear topology such as residual connections or multi-branch models, so those cases require the functional API or subclassing. The site does not state a release date for the remaining distribution backends, does not give a full comparison of backend performance across hardware, and does not address the mathematical prerequisites for advanced work. The facts provided also do not settle questions of long-term support policy, commercial backing or the size of the contributor community beyond the star count and push date.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
